findings.problem: fs::read_to_string(path).unwrap() - unwrap() on file I/O is a panic path that violates the zero-unwrap/zero-panic-by-default rule. File I/O failures (permission denied, missing file, too many open files) will panic the caller.
findings.failure_mode: Process terminates on any file read error with a backtrace dump; no typed error returned to caller.
findings.fix: Return Result<Vec<Reading>, std::io::Error> and use fs::read_to_string(path).map_err(|e| Error::FileRead { path: path.to_owned(), source: e }) or propagate with ?.

findings.problem: parts[1].parse::<u32>().unwrap() - unwrap() on numeric parsing is a panic path. A non-numeric second CSV field will panic. Additionally, casting u32 to u16 with 'as' is an unchecked narrowing conversion that can silently truncate values >= 65536.
findings.failure_mode: Process panics on malformed CSV data, or silently truncates values >= 65536 when parse succeeds but cast loses data. Both are data-corruption or denial-of-service vectors.
findings.fix: Use u16::from_str or .try_into() with proper Error conversion. Replace with: parts[1].trim().parse::<u16>().map_err(|e| Error::ParseValue { field: parts[0].clone(), source: e }) or check range explicitly.

findings.problem: parts[1] - direct indexing into the split result without checking parts.len() >= 2. Similarly parts[0] on line 18 and parts[2] on line 20 are unchecked indexing with no bounds proof.
findings.failure_mode: Index out of bounds panic on malformed CSV lines (e.g., missing columns). Unbounded user input causes process panic - classic denial-of-service vector.
findings.fix: Check parts.len() before indexing. If parts.len() < 3, return a typed parse error rather than panicking. Use parts.get(1) and parts.get(2) with Ok(Err(...)) or match.

findings.problem: println!("loaded {}", parts[0]); - the Result<i32, std::io::Error> from println! is silently ignored. This violates the checked-returns rule (Rule 7). Even in a loader function, ignoring I/O failure is a silent data-loss bug.
findings.failure_mode: Stdout errors are silently swallowed. In a constrained environment (pipe broken, stdout full), loader progress is lost with no indication.
findings.fix: Either remove the println entirely (it is debug output in production code and a performance anti-pattern) or propagate the Result: let _ = writeln!(stdout(), "loaded {}")?; with a proper Result return type.

findings.problem: line.split(',').map(...).collect() allocates a Vec<String> per CSV line inside the loop. Each allocation is a heap allocation after initialization with no declared allocation budget.
findings.failure_mode: Per-line heap allocation causes GC pressure, allocation stall tail latency spikes, and OOM on large files. No allocation budget is declared anywhere in the crate.
findings.fix: Use line.splitn(3, ',') and borrow slices instead of allocating Strings. Use a scratch buffer or caller-provided output buffer. For hot paths, accept &str slices and only allocate for owned return values.

findings.problem: parts[2].split('|').map(|flag| flag.to_string()).collect() allocates another Vec<String> per line for flags. Total per-line allocation: 3 Vec allocations + N String allocations (1 sensor + N-1 flags). No allocation budget is stated.
findings.failure_mode: For a file with 10000 lines and 3 flags each, this creates ~40000 heap allocations (10000 Vec<String> parts + 10000 sensor Strings + 30000 flag Strings). Allocation stalls and OOM are likely on resource-constrained systems.
findings.fix: Return borrowed slices for flags instead of owned Strings, or use a compact representation (e.g., a single String with offset indices, or ArrayVec<[&str; MAX_FLAGS] if MAX_FLAGS is known statically).

findings.problem: text.lines() iterates over all lines in the file with no static upper bound or mathematical termination proof. For safety-critical code (Rule 2), every loop must have a provable bound.
findings.failure_mode: Infinite or runaway processing on very large files. No backpressure, no max-line-count limit. An attacker could supply a massive file and cause resource exhaustion.
findings.fix: Accept a max_lines parameter or return Result with a resource-exhausted error when the file exceeds a configured line limit. Use .take(MAX_LINES) with an explicit constant or bounded iterator wrapper.

findings.problem: 'as u16' cast from u32 is an unchecked narrowing conversion. If parse succeeds with a value >= 65536, the cast silently truncates to (value & 0xFFFF) instead of wrapping or saturating.
findings.failure_mode: Data corruption: sensor reading 70000 becomes 4464 silently. No error is returned; the caller gets a wrong value with no indication of data loss.
findings.fix: Use .try_into() to convert u32 to u16 with proper error handling, or use .saturating_to::<u16>() if truncation-to-max is acceptable, documented clearly.

findings.problem: load_readings returns Vec<Reading> (infallible) for an operation that can fail on file read, parse errors, and I/O errors. There is no Error type defined and no Result return. All error cases manifest as panics via unwrap().
findings.failure_mode: No typed error taxonomy exists. Every failure path is a panic, violating the Railway-Oriented Programming pattern and the checked-returns rule.
findings.fix: Define an Error enum with variants: FileRead(std::io::Error), ParseValue { sensor: String, source: ParseIntError }, MalformedLine { line: usize }. Return Result<Vec<Reading>, Error>.

findings.problem: Reading struct has no validation invariants. sensor can be empty, value has no valid range check, flags can be empty or contain whitespace. Invalid states are representable.
findings.failure_mode: Downstream consumers receive sensors with empty names or unexpected data. No constructor enforces invariants; pub fields allow mutation after construction.
findings.fix: Make fields private, provide a constructor that validates: sensor non-empty, value in valid range (or document u16 as-is). Use a builder or try_from pattern.

findings.problem: println!() in a loader function is a performance anti-pattern in production code. It blocks on stdout, formats a string every time (allocation + syscalls), and pollutes the common path with debug output.
findings.failure_mode: Severely degraded throughput due to blocked stdout I/O. In a high-throughput sensor loading scenario, each println is a syscall that serializes execution.
findings.fix: Remove println entirely. Use tracing::info! with sampling or no logging at all in the hot path. If progress tracking is needed, use a callback or counter metric.

findings.problem: No rust-toolchain.toml exists. The skill requires a checked-in pinned dated nightly toolchain with rustfmt, clippy, rust-src, llvm-tools-preview, and target list components.
findings.failure_mode: Floating toolchain versions cause non-reproducible builds. No access to nightly-only features (portable_simd, try_blocks) or stricter linting.
findings.fix: Create rust-toolchain.toml with a pinned nightly channel (e.g., nightly-2025-01-15), profile = minimal, and required components.

findings.problem: No benchmark dependencies (criterion, iai-callgrind) and no [dev-dependencies] or [dependencies] section. No benchmarks exist for the load_readings function.
findings.failure_mode: No measurement evidence exists for allocation count, latency, or throughput. Performance claims cannot be made. Regressions cannot be detected.
findings.fix: Add criterion = '0.5' to [dev-dependencies] and create a benchmarks/load_readings.rs with benchmarks for varying file sizes, reporting allocations/iter and bytes/iter.

findings.problem: No tests exist in the crate. No test targets, no #[cfg(test)] module, no test files. The gate requires cargo test to compile and run.
findings.failure_mode: No test evidence exists for correctness. Edge cases (empty file, single column, malformed CSV, large values) are untested.
findings.fix: Add #[cfg(test)] mod tests with: test_empty_file, test_single_reading, test_multiple_readings, test_missing_column, test_non_numeric_value, test_large_value, test_flags_parsing.

findings.problem: No [profile.release] section defined. The skill requires a release profile with opt-level = 3, lto = thin, codegen-units = 1, strip = symbols.
findings.failure_mode: Default debug profile is used for builds unless explicitly overridden. Performance and code-size measurements are meaningless against debug builds.
findings.fix: Add [profile.release] with opt-level = 3, lto = thin, codegen-units = 1, strip = symbols.

findings.problem: load_readings at 14 lines (10-23) is close to the 25-line target, but the single function handles file I/O, CSV parsing, numeric parsing, logging, and collection - five distinct responsibilities in one function.
findings.failure_mode: Single-point-of-failure function that is hard to test, hard to verify, and hard to optimize. Violates the spirit of smallest-scope and function simplicity rules.
findings.fix: Split into: read_file(path) -> Result<String>, parse_reading(line: &str) -> Result<Reading>, load_readings(content: &str) -> Result<Vec<Reading>>.

missing_evidence: no benchmark exists: no criterion/iai-callgrind dependency, no bench target, no latency/throughput measurements for load_readings
no profiler evidence: no flamegraph, perf stat, or cachegrind data showing allocation hotspots or CPU bottlenecks
no assembly/IR evidence: no cargo asm, cargo llvm-ir output to verify LLVM inlining or bounds-check removal
no second-ring tools: no Crux, SAW, Hax, Miri, or Kani evidence; no UB or concurrency verification
no rust-toolchain.toml: pinned nightly toolchain not present for zero-slippage gate
no tests: zero test coverage means no behavior test evidence
no dependency audit: no cargo audit, cargo deny, cargo geiger evidence (no dependencies but also no audit gate config)
no allocation budget statement: hot path allocates ~3 Vecs + N Strings per line with no declared budget
residual_risk: The crate is a single-file loader with 16 BLOCKER-level violations. Every execution path that encounters malformed input, I/O errors, or large files will panic. There are zero tests, zero benchmarks, zero error types, zero allocation budget, and no toolchain pinning. The code would need a complete rewrite with proper error handling (Result return type, typed Error enum), checked indexing (parts.get() with error conversion), unchecked cast elimination (try_into for u32->u16), allocation reduction (borrowed slices or caller-owned buffers), loop bounds, removal of println, and a full test/benchmark suite before it could pass a Holzman Rust review gate. As-is, it fails all three gate categories: correctness, performance budget, and allocation budget.
